body: For an action \[ S[\phi]\coloneqq\int\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a,x)\,d^4x, \] the variational calculation gives \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial \phi_a}-\partial_\mu\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}\right)\overset{\text{stationary action}}{=}0. \] The \(\text{stationary action}\) label marks that this field equation is imposed by requiring the first variation of the field action to vanish. This is the field version of the \cref{Euler-Lagrange equations}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations}.

title: Why a derivative moves
body: The variation contains a term proportional to \(\partial_\mu\delta\phi_a\). Integrating by parts moves \(\partial_\mu\) onto \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\). The boundary term vanishes because the field variation is fixed at the boundary.

title: Local partial differential equations
body: Field equations are usually partial differential equations. They relate a field and its spacetime derivatives at neighbouring events, expressing local compatibility rather than instantaneous influence from distant places.

title: The wave-operator pattern
body: Relativistic equations often contain the d'Alembertian \(\Box\coloneqq\partial_\mu\partial^\mu\). With explicit \(c\), \[ \Box\overset{\text{components}}{=}\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2. \] The \(\text{components}\) label marks the expansion of the covariant operator in the chosen coordinate convention. Its sign structure reflects spacetime geometry and finite-speed propagation.

title: Maxwell as the central example
body: \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations} are the main field equations in this atlas. In covariant form they relate derivatives of the electromagnetic field tensor to the four-current source.

title: Not just a global constraint
body: A field equation is not merely a statement about a total quantity over all space. It is a local rule: at each event, the field and its derivatives must satisfy a differential relation.

title: Field equations before relativity
body: Maxwell's nineteenth-century equations already had the character of local field equations. Special relativity later revealed their covariant spacetime structure and made such equations the model for modern field theory.

title: Takeaway
body: Field equations are local differential equations obtained from an action or other physical principle. They tell fields how to vary consistently through spacetime.

title: The potential behind the field
body: The electromagnetic vector potential \(A_\mu\) is the spacetime field whose derivatives build the observable electromagnetic field. It is central because relativity and the action principle handle it cleanly.

title: Definition
body: The vector potential \(A_\mu\) is an electromagnetic \cref{Vector field}{sr.vector_field} assigning components at each \cref{Spacetime event}{sr.spacetime_event}. With one common convention, \(A^\mu\coloneqq(\phi/c,\mathbf A)\) and \(A_\mu\coloneqq(\phi/c,-\mathbf A)\), where \(\phi\) is the scalar potential and \(\mathbf A\) the three-vector potential.

title: From potential to field strength
body:
The electromagnetic field tensor is built from the antisymmetric derivative \[ F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu. \] The definition sign marks the local potential convention used here; this construction defines the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and packages the electric and magnetic fields covariantly.

title: Why the antisymmetric derivative
body: The difference \(\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu\) keeps the curl-like part of the potential's variation. It leaves six independent components, matching the three electric and three magnetic components, and it removes pure-gradient changes.

title: Gauge freedom
body: Different potentials can describe the same electromagnetic field. A transformation \(A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\) leaves \(F_{\mu\nu}\) unchanged, which is the seed of \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance}.

title: Field variable in the action
body: In the electromagnetic \cref{Field Lagrangian}{sr.field_lagrangian}, the potential \(A_\mu\) is the field varied in the action. This route gives a compact way to derive the sourced Maxwell equations.

title: Coupling to charge
body: A charged particle couples locally to the potential through a term proportional to \(qA_\mu dx^\mu\). This scalar worldline coupling is one reason \(A_\mu\), not just \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\), becomes structurally important.

title: Not simply the observed field
body: The vector potential is not directly the electric or magnetic field introduced in elementary electromagnetism. The observable field strength is built from derivatives of \(A_\mu\), and many potentials can correspond to the same field tensor.

title: Potentials become central
body: Potentials began as useful calculational devices in classical electromagnetism. Relativistic and quantum formulations made them structurally central, especially because the four-potential couples naturally in the action.

title: Takeaway
body: The vector potential is the local four-vector field from which \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is constructed. Its gauge freedom makes it redundant as a description, but powerful as a dynamical variable.

title: One tensor for electromagnetism
body: The electromagnetic field tensor \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is the covariant object that packages electric and magnetic field components into one relativistic field strength.

title: Definition
body:
The field tensor is the antisymmetric tensor constructed from the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential}: \[ F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu,\qquad F_{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{antisymmetry}}{=}-F_{
u\mu}. \] The definition sign marks the local potential convention used in this atlas. The \(	ext{antisymmetry}\) label marks the consequence of swapping the two derivative terms. Signs and factors are fixed only after the potential and coordinate conventions are fixed. It represents the electromagnetic field in covariant form.

title: Antisymmetry
body: Antisymmetry makes all diagonal components vanish and pairs off the off-diagonal components with opposite signs. In four dimensions, this leaves \(4\cdot3/2=6\) independent components.

title: Why six is suggestive
body: Six independent components match the three components of the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and the three components of the \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}. The tensor does not add new classical field components; it repackages them covariantly.

title: The frame split
body: After choosing an inertial frame, the time-space components of \(F_{\mu\nu}\) are identified with electric-field components, while the purely spatial antisymmetric components are identified with magnetic-field components. Signs and factors of \(c\) depend on convention.

title: Index placement matters
body: Indices on \(F_{\mu\nu}\) are raised and lowered with the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}. With a \(+---\) convention, raising spatial indices can introduce signs. A calculation must keep one convention fixed throughout.

title: Why electric and magnetic mix
body: A Lorentz boost mixes time and space directions. Since electric components are time-space parts of \(F_{\mu\nu}\) and magnetic components are space-space parts, a boost can mix what observers call electric and magnetic.

title: Built-in homogeneous structure
body: Because \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is constructed as an antisymmetric derivative of \(A_\mu\), the cyclic derivative identity follows from commuting partial derivatives. This becomes the homogeneous half of \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}.

title: Not two unrelated fields
body: The tensor view does not treat \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) as two independent substances. They are observer-dependent components of one electromagnetic field tensor.

title: Minkowski's electromagnetic form
body: After Einstein's special relativity, Minkowski's spacetime formulation made it natural to write electromagnetism with four-dimensional tensors. The field tensor is one of the cleanest examples of that reorganisation.

title: Takeaway
body: \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is the covariant electromagnetic field strength. It is built from the potential, has six independent components, and makes the unity of electric and magnetic fields explicit.

title: The field seen by charges at rest
body: The electric field is the part of the electromagnetic field that acts on a charge instantaneously at rest in a chosen inertial frame. Relativistically, it is a frame-dependent reading of the field tensor.

title: Definition
body: The electric field \(\mathbf E\) is the three-vector field measured in a chosen \cref{Inertial frames}{sr.inertial_frames} by the force per unit charge on a test charge at rest in that frame. In covariant notation it is read from the time-space components of the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}.

title: A chosen frame is part of the statement
body: The phrase electric field silently includes an observer's split of spacetime into time plus space. Another inertial observer may decompose the same electromagnetic field tensor into different electric and magnetic components.

title: Time-space components
body: Choose a frame and write \(F_{\mu\nu}\) in time and space parts. The components with one time index and one spatial index, conventionally \(F_{0i}\) or \(F^{0i}\), contain the electric field up to signs and factors fixed by the chosen convention.

title: From potentials
body: In ordinary three-vector notation, the electric field is recovered from the scalar and vector potentials by \[ \mathbf E\overset{\text{potentials}}{=}-\nabla\phi-\frac{\partial\mathbf A}{\partial t}. \] The \(\text{potentials}\) label marks the chosen potential convention. The first term comes from spatial variation of the scalar potential; the second from time variation of the vector potential.

title: Static potential example
body: If \(\mathbf A\) is time-independent and the scalar potential decreases in the \(+x\) direction, then \(E_x\overset{\text{static}}{=}-\partial\phi/\partial x\) points toward increasing potential drop. The \(\text{static}\) label marks that the time-derivative term in the potential formula has dropped out. This recovers the elementary electrostatic picture inside the tensor formalism.

title: Force meaning
body: A positive test charge at rest accelerates along \(\mathbf E\). This operational meaning is frame-specific, but it is often the most concrete way to understand what the electric part of the field does.

title: Not absolute by itself
body: It is misleading to ask for the electric field without specifying the frame when relativistic motion matters. The invariant object is the electromagnetic field tensor, while \(\mathbf E\) is one frame's decomposition of it.

title: From electrostatics to field components
body: The electric field entered physics through electrostatic forces and Faraday's field picture. Special relativity later placed that familiar field inside a larger electromagnetic tensor.

title: Takeaway
body: The electric field is physically concrete, but not relativistically standalone. It is the time-space part of \(F_{\mu\nu}\) after an inertial frame has been chosen.

title: The field tied to motion and current
body: The magnetic field is the frame-dependent part of the electromagnetic field associated with currents and sideways forces on moving charges. In tensor language it lives in the spatial antisymmetric components.

title: Definition
body: The magnetic field \(\mathbf B\) is the three-vector field read, in a chosen inertial frame, from the purely spatial components of the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}. It is associated operationally with forces on moving charges and with currents.

title: Spatial antisymmetry
body: The spatial entries \(F_{ij}\) form an antisymmetric \(3\times3\) block. In three spatial dimensions, such an antisymmetric block has three independent components, which can be encoded as the components of \(\mathbf B\).

title: From the vector potential
body: In ordinary three-vector notation the magnetic field is the curl of the vector potential: \[ \mathbf B\overset{\text{potentials}}{=}\nabla\times\mathbf A. \] The \(\text{potentials}\) label marks the chosen potential convention. This is the spatial part of the antisymmetric derivative used in \(F_{\mu\nu}\).

title: Sideways force
body: In the familiar Lorentz-force expression, the magnetic part acts through \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\). This makes magnetic force depend on the motion of the test charge in the chosen frame.

title: Current-carrying wire
body: A steady current in a wire produces circular magnetic field lines around the wire in the lab frame. Relativity teaches that another frame may describe the same physical situation with a different mixture of electric and magnetic components.

title: Frame-dependent split
body: Like the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field}, the magnetic field is not an invariant object by itself. It is part of an observer's decomposition of the electromagnetic field tensor.

title: A hint of no magnetic monopoles
body: The formula \(\mathbf B\overset{\text{potentials}}{=}\nabla\times\mathbf A\) immediately gives \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf B\overset{\text{curl}}{=}0\) for smooth potentials, because the divergence of a curl vanishes. The \(\text{curl}\) label marks that mathematical identity. This is one of the homogeneous Maxwell equations.

title: Not a separate substance
body: The magnetic field should not be treated as an independent relativistic substance alongside the electric field. Both are frame-dependent faces of one electromagnetic tensor.

title: From magnetism to electromagnetism
body: Magnetic effects were known long before relativity. Maxwell unified magnetism with electricity dynamically; special relativity then explained the electric/magnetic split as observer-dependent.

title: Takeaway
body: The magnetic field is the spatial part of \(F_{\mu\nu}\) in a chosen frame. It is tied to currents and moving charges, and it transforms together with the electric field under changes of inertial frame.

title: One field, two frame faces
body: The electromagnetic field is the unified relativistic field whose frame-dependent faces are the electric and magnetic fields. The covariant representative is the field tensor.

title: Definition
body: The electromagnetic field is the physical field represented covariantly by the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}. In a chosen frame, its components are decomposed into the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} \(\mathbf E\) and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field} \(\mathbf B\).

title: The six-component package
body: The three electric components and three magnetic components are the six independent components of the antisymmetric tensor \(F_{\mu\nu}\). The tensor is the package; \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) are one observer's unpacking.

title: Observer-dependent decomposition
body: To speak of electric and magnetic parts, an observer chooses a time direction and spatial slice. Another observer moving relative to the first chooses a different split of spacetime and can read different \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) components from the same tensor.

title: Lorentz mixing
body: Under \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}, time-space and space-space tensor components mix. This is the relativistic reason electric and magnetic fields transform into one another under boosts.

title: A local physical field
body: The electromagnetic field assigns field strength locally throughout spacetime. It replaces instantaneous action at a distance with local field values and local differential equations.

title: Energy and momentum
body: The electromagnetic field is not merely a force bookkeeping device. It carries energy and momentum, later described by field energy density, the Poynting vector, and the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor.

title: Not electricity plus magnetism glued together
body: The relativistic view is not two separate fields awkwardly combined. It is one electromagnetic field whose electric/magnetic split depends on the observer.

title: Maxwell, Einstein, Minkowski
body: Maxwell unified electricity, magnetism, and light dynamically. Einstein's relativity and Minkowski's spacetime geometry then made the unity structurally explicit through covariant fields and tensors.

title: Takeaway
body: The electromagnetic field is one local relativistic field. \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) are important frame-dependent descriptions, while \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is the compact covariant object.

title: Local laws of electromagnetism
body: Maxwell's equations are the local field equations for electromagnetism. In relativistic form they are compact equations for the field tensor and four-current.

title: Definition
body: Maxwell's equations govern the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. In covariant notation they relate the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} to the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current} and impose the homogeneous identity satisfied by the field tensor.

title: Sourced equation
body: The sourced covariant equation is \[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{Maxwell}}{=}\mu_0 j^\nu \] in SI-style conventions. The \(\text{Maxwell}\) label marks this as a field law, not an algebraic identity. It says local charge-current density sources derivatives of the electromagnetic field.

title: Homogeneous equation
body:
The homogeneous covariant equation is \[ \partial_\lambda F_{\mu
u}+\partial_\mu F_{
u\lambda}+\partial_
u F_{\lambda\mu}\overset{	ext{homogeneous}}{=}0. \] The \(	ext{homogeneous}\) label marks the source-free identity that follows from constructing \(F_{\mu
u}\) as an antisymmetric derivative of a potential.

title: From the field action
body:
Maxwell's sourced equation follows by applying the \cref{Euler-Lagrange equations}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations} to the electromagnetic \cref{Field Lagrangian}{sr.field_lagrangian}, for example \[ \mathcal L\coloneqq- rac{1}{4\mu_0}F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}-j_\mu A^\mu. \] The definition sign marks a conventional electromagnetic Lagrangian density. Varying the potential gives \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{stationary action}}{=}\mu_0j^
u\), up to convention.

title: Why the homogeneous part cancels
body:
Substitute \(F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\) into the cyclic derivative expression. The result contains pairs of second derivatives with opposite signs. For smooth fields, partial derivatives commute, so each pair cancels.

title: The usual four equations
body: After choosing a frame, the covariant pair becomes the familiar Gauss law for electricity, Gauss law for magnetism, Faraday induction law, and Ampere-Maxwell law. The covariant form shows why those four equations belong together.

title: Consistency with charge conservation
body:
Taking the divergence of the sourced equation gives \(\partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{Maxwell}}{=}\mu_0\partial_
u j^
u\). The \(	ext{Maxwell}\) label marks use of the sourced field equation. The left side vanishes by antisymmetry, implying \cref{Charge conservation}{sr.charge_conservation}: \(\partial_\mu j^\mu\overset{	ext{charge conservation}}{=}0\).

title: Source-free waves
body: In regions with \(j^\mu\overset{\text{source-free}}{=}0\), Maxwell's equations still allow nonzero propagating solutions. The \(\text{source-free}\) label marks a physical condition on the source, not the absence of the electromagnetic field. This leads to \cref{Electromagnetic waves}{sr.electromagnetic_waves} and to the \cref{Wave equation}{sr.wave_equation} for fields or potentials in suitable gauges.

title: Not four unrelated formulas
body: The familiar four equations are not a disconnected list. They are frame components of compact covariant field equations plus the geometric construction of the field tensor.

title: Maxwell and light
body: Maxwell's nineteenth-century synthesis showed that electricity and magnetism imply waves travelling at the speed of light. Special relativity later made the equations' spacetime covariance central to their interpretation.

title: Takeaway
body: Maxwell's equations are the local relativistic field equations of electromagnetism. They connect sources to fields, encode the homogeneous identities, enforce charge conservation, and permit light-like waves.

title: A covariant gauge choice
body: The Lorenz gauge is a particularly useful way to choose a representative electromagnetic potential while preserving the relativistic form of the equations.

title: Definition
body: The Lorenz gauge is the condition \[ \partial_\mu A^\mu\overset{\text{Lorenz gauge}}{=}0 \] imposed on the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential}. The \(\text{Lorenz gauge}\) label marks a gauge choice, not a new physical law. It is a specific example of \cref{Gauge fixing}{sr.gauge_fixing}.

title: Why a gauge condition is allowed
body: Because of \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance}, many potentials describe the same \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. A gauge condition chooses one representative from that family; it should simplify calculation without changing \(F_{\mu\nu}\).

title: Why this gauge is relativistic
body: The quantity \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\) is a scalar contraction. If it is zero in one inertial frame, it is zero in every Lorentz-related inertial frame. That is why the Lorenz gauge is compatible with the relativistic form of electrodynamics.

title: Maxwell equations become wave equations
body:
In potential form, the sourced \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations} contain a term of the schematic form \[ \Box A^
u-\partial^
u(\partial_\mu A^\mu)\overset{	ext{Maxwell}}{=}\mu_0j^
u. \] The \(	ext{Maxwell}\) label marks that this is the sourced field equation rewritten in terms of the potential. Imposing \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\overset{	ext{Lorenz gauge}}{=}0\) removes the second term, leaving a wave equation for each component of the potential, up to sign and unit conventions. The \(	ext{Lorenz gauge}\) label marks the condition being used to simplify the potential equation.

title: It may not fix everything
body: The Lorenz gauge need not remove all gauge freedom. A further transformation \(A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\) preserves the condition when \(\Box\Lambda\overset{\text{residual gauge}}{=}0\). The \(\text{residual gauge}\) label marks the extra condition on the gauge function. This remaining freedom matters in some calculations.

title: Not a new physical law
body: The Lorenz gauge is not an additional law of nature. It is a choice of description within a gauge-equivalent family of potentials. The physical field remains \(F_{\mu\nu}\).

title: Lorenz, not Lorentz
body: The gauge is named after Ludvig Lorenz. It is often confused with Hendrik Lorentz because the condition is Lorentz-covariant and appears constantly in relativistic electrodynamics.

title: Takeaway
body: The Lorenz gauge imposes \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\overset{\text{Lorenz gauge}}{=}0\). It is a covariant gauge choice that simplifies Maxwell's equations for the vector potential into wave-equation form.

title: Redundancy without physical change
body: Gauge invariance is the statement that some changes in the electromagnetic potential change the description but not the physical electromagnetic field.

title: Definition
body: Electromagnetic gauge invariance is the freedom to transform the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} by \[ A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda \] without changing the physical \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. The \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} remains unchanged.

title: Why \(F_{\mu\nu}\) is unchanged
body:
Substitute \(A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\) into \(F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\). The added part is \[ \partial_\mu\partial_
u\Lambda-\partial_
u\partial_\mu\Lambda\overset{	ext{commuting partials}}{=}0, \] which vanishes for smooth \(\Lambda\). The \(	ext{commuting partials}\) label marks the mathematical identity responsible for gauge invariance.

title: Many descriptions, one field
body: Gauge-related potentials are different mathematical representatives of the same physical field tensor. This is not a new force or hidden disturbance; it is redundancy in the potential description.

title: Not every change in \(A_\mu\) is physical
body: It is tempting to think that changing a field variable must change the physical situation. Gauge invariance says otherwise: a pure-gradient change of \(A_\mu\) can leave \(F_{\mu\nu}\), and hence all classical electromagnetic fields, unchanged.

title: Observable quantities
body: In classical electromagnetism the directly physical field strength is \(F_{\mu\nu}\), or equivalently the frame-dependent \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\). The potential \(A_\mu\) is structurally important, but its gauge-dependent parts are not separately observable.

title: Why gauge fixing exists
body: Because many potentials represent the same field, calculations often impose an extra condition to choose one representative. That later step is \cref{Gauge fixing}{sr.gauge_fixing}; it simplifies description without changing the electromagnetic field.

title: Constraint on interactions
body: Gauge invariance also constrains how charged matter couples to electromagnetism. \cref{Minimal coupling}{sr.minimal_coupling} is arranged so that gauge changes in the potential do not change physical predictions.

title: From potential freedom to gauge theory
body: The freedom in electromagnetic potentials was first a feature of classical field descriptions. In twentieth-century physics it became a central organising principle for interactions, far beyond classical electromagnetism.

title: Takeaway
body: Gauge invariance says that the electromagnetic potential contains descriptive redundancy. The field tensor is unchanged by \(A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\), so physics depends on gauge-invariant structure.

title: Charge flow as a four-vector
body: The four-current packages charge density and current density into one relativistic source object. It is the source that appears in covariant Maxwell equations.

title: Definition
body: The four-current is the \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors} \[ j^\mu\coloneqq(c\rho,\mathbf j), \] where \(\rho\) is charge density and \(\mathbf j\) is ordinary current density. It is the source term in covariant \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}.

title: Why \(c\rho\)
body: Multiplying charge density by \(c\) gives the time component the same dimensional character as current density: charge per area per time. It also fits the four-vector transformation law.

title: Charge density alone is not enough
body: Different observers can disagree about charge density and current density for moving charges. The separate quantities \(\rho\) and \(\mathbf j\) mix between frames; the covariant source is \(j^\mu\).

title: Local charge flow
body: The time component tells how much charge is locally present. The spatial components tell how charge flows through a small surface. Together they describe charge moving through spacetime.

title: Four-divergence and conservation
body: Local \cref{Charge conservation}{sr.charge_conservation} is written compactly as \[ \partial_\mu j^\mu\overset{\text{charge conservation}}{=}0. \] The \(\text{charge conservation}\) label marks this as the local conservation law for charge. Expanding this gives the ordinary continuity equation \(\partial\rho/\partial t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\overset{\text{continuity}}{=}0\).

title: Source for the field
body: In covariant electromagnetism, the sourced Maxwell equation has the schematic form \[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{Maxwell}}{=}\mu_0 j^\nu. \] The \(\text{Maxwell}\) label marks the field equation that makes the four-current the local source for the electromagnetic field.

title: Wire intuition
body: A current-carrying wire can be described by a charge density and a current density in the lab frame. A frame moving with some charges assigns different component values, but the four-current keeps the descriptions related.

title: Sources made covariant
body: Classical electromagnetism already used charge and current as sources. Relativity reorganised them into one four-vector, matching the four-dimensional form of the electromagnetic field equations.

title: Takeaway
body: The four-current is local charge flow written covariantly. It packages \(\rho\) and \(\mathbf j\), sources Maxwell's equations, and expresses charge conservation through \(\partial_\mu j^\mu\overset{\text{charge conservation}}{=}0\).

title: The economical electromagnetic interaction
body: Minimal coupling is the standard way to introduce electromagnetic interaction into a charged particle's dynamics using the least extra local structure compatible with gauge invariance.

title: Definition
body: Minimal coupling introduces the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} into a charged particle's action or momentum structure, commonly through the gauge-covariant combination \[ p_\mu-eA_\mu. \] It is guided by \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance}.

title: What minimal means
body: Minimal does not mean physically unimportant. It means the simplest local coupling is used: add the potential in the direct way required for a charge, without adding extra higher-order or nonlocal interaction terms.

title: Worldline coupling
body: For a charged particle, the interaction term can be written proportionally to \[ eA_\mu dx^\mu. \] The contraction \(A_\mu dx^\mu\) is a Lorentz scalar, so it fits naturally into a relativistic action.

title: Momentum replacement
body: In momentum language the same idea is expressed by replacing free momentum structure with a potential-dependent combination such as \(p_\mu-eA_\mu\). The exact sign convention depends on the charge and index convention.

title: Gauge compatibility
body: The coupling must not make gauge-related potentials predict different physics. Minimal coupling is arranged so that gauge changes can be compensated by the corresponding change in the charged particle description.

title: Canonical versus mechanical momentum
body: In the nonrelativistic limit, a charged-particle Lagrangian contains terms involving \(\phi\) and \(\mathbf A\). The canonical momentum can therefore include potential-dependent pieces, while mechanical momentum tracks motion.

title: Toward the force law
body: Varying the minimally coupled action gives the \cref{Lorentz force law}{sr.lorentz_force_law}. The antisymmetric derivative of the potential appears in the calculation and combines into the field tensor \(F_{\mu\nu}\).

title: Not an arbitrary substitution trick
body: Minimal coupling is not a mnemonic inserted after the fact. It encodes locality, Lorentz covariance, charge, and gauge compatibility in the action or momentum structure.

title: A bridge to modern gauge theory
body: The coupling of charged particles to electromagnetic potentials became a prototype for how interactions are introduced in gauge theories. Later quantum theory made this structural role even more prominent.

title: Takeaway
body: Minimal coupling introduces electromagnetic interaction by coupling charge locally to \(A_\mu\). It is economical, gauge-compatible, and leads to the Lorentz force law.

title: How fields move charges
body: The Lorentz force law is the rule that turns an electromagnetic field into the motion of a charged particle.

title: Definition
Three-vector form
body: In an inertial frame, the spatial part becomes the familiar expression \[ \mathbf F\overset{\text{3-vector}}{=}q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B). \] The \(\text{3-vector}\) label marks the frame-dependent decomposition of the covariant force law. The electric field contributes a force along \(\mathbf E\), while the magnetic field contributes a velocity-dependent sideways force.

title: From the action
body: The law follows by applying the \cref{Action principle}{sr.action_principle} to a charged particle with \cref{Minimal coupling}{sr.minimal_coupling}. The particle path is varied, and the potential sampled along that path changes with the variation.

title: Why the field tensor appears
body:
In the worldline variation, derivative terms from the potential combine as \[ \partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu. \] This antisymmetric combination is precisely \(F_{\mu
u}\), so the final force law depends on the field tensor rather than on a gauge-dependent part of the potential.

title: Electric and magnetic roles
body: Electric and magnetic forces look different in a chosen frame. An electric field can accelerate a charge along or against the field. A magnetic field acts through \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\), so it vanishes for a charge at rest and is perpendicular to the velocity in the simple magnetic-only case.

title: Power delivered to the particle
body: Taking the dot product of the three-vector law with \(\mathbf v\) gives \[ \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\overset{\text{Lorentz force}}{=}q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v+q(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf v. \] The \(\text{Lorentz force}\) label marks substitution of the three-vector force law. The magnetic term is zero because \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf v\). Thus, in this frame, the electric field is the part that changes the particle's energy directly.

title: Conventions matter
body: Signs and factors of \(c\) depend on metric signature, index placement, charge convention, and the chosen definitions of \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) inside \(F_{\mu\nu}\). The physical content is the same when all conventions are used consistently.

title: Not the whole story for an emitting charge
body: The Lorentz force law describes the force exerted by an electromagnetic field on a charge. It does not by itself solve the harder problem of a charge reacting to its own emitted radiation; that later issue is radiation reaction.

title: Lorentz's synthesis
body: The force law is named for Hendrik Lorentz, whose electron theory helped connect electromagnetic fields, charged particles, and the transformations that later became central to special relativity.

title: Takeaway
body: The Lorentz force law says that \(F_{\mu\nu}\) acting on a charged particle's four-velocity changes its four-momentum. In a chosen frame this contains the familiar electric force and magnetic deflection.

title: Local bookkeeping
body: Charge conservation says more than that the total charge stays fixed. It says charge can leave a region only by flowing through its boundary.

title: Definition
body: The local relativistic statement of charge conservation is the continuity equation for the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current}: \[ \partial_\mu j^\mu \overset{\text{charge conservation}}{=} 0. \] In ordinary vector notation the four-divergence expands as \[ \partial_\mu j^\mu \equiv \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j, \] so the same conservation law is \[ \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\overset{\text{continuity}}{=}0. \] The \(\text{continuity}\) label marks the ordinary vector form of the same local conservation law.

title: What the equation says
body: If \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\) is positive at a point, more current is flowing out than in, so the charge density there decreases. If it is negative, current is converging and the charge density increases.

title: From local to integral form
body: Define the charge inside a fixed volume by \(Q_V\coloneqq\int_V\rho\,d^3x\). Integrating the local continuity equation over \(V\) gives \[ \frac{d}{dt}\int_V\rho\,d^3x \overset{\text{continuity}}{=} -\int_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\,d^3x. \] By the divergence theorem this becomes \[ \frac{dQ_V}{dt} \overset{\text{Gauss theorem}}{=} -\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf j\cdot d\mathbf a. \] The charge inside changes by the negative of the outward current flux.

title: Consistency of Maxwell's equations
body:
Charge conservation follows from the sourced \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}. The sourced equation is \[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu
u} \overset{	ext{Maxwell}}{=} \mu_0j^
u. \] Taking its divergence gives \[ \partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u} \overset{	ext{Maxwell}}{=} \mu_0\partial_
u j^
u. \] The left side vanishes because \(F^{\mu
u}\) is antisymmetric while the double derivative is symmetric, leaving \[ \partial_
u j^
u\overset{	ext{charge conservation}}{=}0. \] The \(	ext{charge conservation}\) label marks the local continuity condition forced by Maxwell consistency.

title: Why antisymmetry matters
body:
The key mathematical fact is that a symmetric object contracted with an antisymmetric object gives zero. Let \(C\coloneqq\partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}\). Since partial derivatives commute, \(\partial_
u\partial_\mu\) is symmetric in the two indices. The field tensor changes sign when those indices are swapped, so \[ C \overset{\mu\leftrightarrow
u}{=} -C. \] Therefore \(C\overset{C=-C}{=}0\). The \(C=-C\) label marks the final consequence of the antisymmetry argument.

title: Not just a global rule
body: A global statement such as \"the total charge is constant\" is weaker than the continuity equation. The local equation forbids charge from disappearing here and reappearing elsewhere without a current connecting the two events.

title: Sources must be compatible
body: In Maxwell theory the current \(j^\mu\) cannot be chosen arbitrarily. A source with nonzero four-divergence would be inconsistent with the antisymmetric field equation.

title: From circuits to fields
body: Conservation of electric charge was first familiar from electrical and chemical phenomena. Field theory sharpens it into a local continuity equation tied to the structure of Maxwell's equations.

title: Takeaway
body: Charge conservation is the local continuity equation \(\partial_\mu j^\mu\overset{\text{charge conservation}}{=}0\). It says charge is neither created nor destroyed at a point; it is transported by current.

title: Energy stored in fields
body: Electromagnetic fields can store energy locally, even in a region where no charged particles are present.

title: Definition
body: The energy density of the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field} is energy per unit volume. In SI units, \[ u\overset{\text{SI}}{=}\frac12\left(\epsilon_0E^2+\frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2\right), \] where \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) are the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}. The \(\text{SI}\) label marks the unit convention built into the constants \(\epsilon_0\) and \(\mu_0\).

title: The \(T^{00}\) component
body: In a chosen inertial frame, electromagnetic energy density is the time-time component of the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}: \[ T^{00}\overset{\text{frame}}{=}u. \] The \(\text{frame}\) label marks that this component identification depends on the observer's time-space split. Substituting the electric and magnetic parts of the field tensor gives the squared-field formula.

title: Why squared fields appear
body: Reversing the sign of \(\mathbf E\) or \(\mathbf B\) should not make stored energy negative. The leading local quantities with the right behaviour are \(E^2\) and \(B^2\). Doubling a field strength quadruples this contribution to the energy density.

title: Energy beyond particles
body: The energy is not only in charged particles. It can be stored in the field between them and can later flow through space. This is essential for understanding radiation and momentum carried by light.

title: Plane-wave balance
body: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic contributions to the energy density are equal in SI units. The field energy is shared between the two components while the wave propagates.

title: Energy density is frame-dependent
body: \[ u\overset{\text{frame}}{=}T^{00}. \] The \(\text{frame}\) label marks that this is the energy density measured in a chosen inertial frame. Another observer decomposes the same stress-energy tensor differently, so energy density by itself is not the whole covariant story.

title: Not just potential energy between charges
body: Field energy is not merely a bookkeeping trick for pairs of charges. In field theory it is locally distributed and can be transported, as electromagnetic waves make especially vivid.

title: Maxwell's field energy
body: The idea that electromagnetic fields themselves store energy was part of the shift from action-at-a-distance thinking to field theory. It became central once light was understood as an electromagnetic wave.

title: Takeaway
body: Electromagnetic energy density is \(u\overset{\text{SI}}{=}\frac12(\epsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)\) in SI units. It is the \(T^{00}\) component measured in a chosen frame.

title: Energy in motion
body: The Poynting vector tells us where energy in the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field} is flowing and links that flow to electromagnetic momentum.

title: Definition
body: In SI units the Poynting vector is \[ \mathbf S\overset{\text{SI}}{=}\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B. \] The \(\text{SI}\) label marks the unit convention responsible for the factor \(1/\mu_0\). It is the electromagnetic energy flux: energy crossing unit area per unit time.

title: Direction from a cross product
body: The cross product \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) points perpendicular to both fields. In a plane wave with \(\mathbf E\) along \(y\) and \(\mathbf B\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf S\) points along \(x\), the propagation direction.

title: Flux, not stored energy
body: Energy density says how much electromagnetic energy is present in a small volume. The Poynting vector says how quickly that energy flows through a surface and in which direction.

title: Origin in the energy-momentum tensor
body: The Poynting vector appears in the mixed time-space components of the electromagnetic \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. When those components are written using the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}, the vector \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) appears.

title: Momentum density
body: In SI units the electromagnetic momentum density is \[ \mathbf g\overset{\text{SI}}{=}\frac{\mathbf S}{c^2}. \] The \(\text{SI}\) label marks the conventional SI relation between field momentum density and energy flux. In natural units, \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), energy flux and momentum density have the same numerical content up to convention-dependent component placement.

title: Radiation pressure
body: A beam of light can push on matter because the field carries momentum as well as energy. Absorbing or reflecting the beam transfers electromagnetic momentum to the material surface.

title: Unit conventions
body: The factor \(1/\mu_0\) belongs to SI units. In natural or Heaviside-Lorentz units the formula is cleaner. Always check the unit convention before comparing formulas.

title: Not a stream of little arrows
body: \(\mathbf S\) is a field quantity, not a literal set of particles flowing along drawn arrows. The arrows represent local energy flux; their interpretation depends on the field configuration.

title: Poynting's theorem
body: John Henry Poynting introduced the energy-flow vector in the 1880s. The result made electromagnetic energy transport a precise local field concept.

title: Takeaway
body: The Poynting vector \(\mathbf S\) gives electromagnetic energy flux. Relativity ties it to field momentum density through \(\mathbf g\overset{\text{SI}}{=}\mathbf S/c^2\) in SI units.

title: The field's accounting tensor
body: The electromagnetic stress-energy tensor is the complete local accounting object for electromagnetic energy, momentum, flux, and stress.

title: Definition
body: The electromagnetic stress-energy tensor is the electromagnetic-field instance of the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. It packages energy density, momentum density, energy flux, and stresses into one Lorentz-covariant object.

title: Tensor formula
body:
It is constructed from the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}. With the \(+---\) convention and suppressing unit-dependent constants, one common form is \[ T^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{EM tensor}}{=}-F^{\mu\lambda}F^
u{}_{\lambda}+ rac14\eta^{\mu
u}F^{\alpha eta}F_{\alpha eta}. \] The \(	ext{EM tensor}\) label marks the electromagnetic stress-energy construction in the stated convention.

title: Why it is quadratic
body: Electromagnetic energy should not change sign if the field is reversed. The simplest Lorentz-covariant expressions with that property are quadratic contractions of \(F_{\mu\nu}\), while the two free indices let the result describe flow and stress as well as density.

title: Component meaning
body: In a chosen inertial frame, \(T^{00}\) is field energy density. Mixed time-space components describe energy flux and momentum density. Spatial-spatial components describe stresses: momentum crossing surfaces.

title: Stress and pressure
body: Radiation pressure is a concrete example of electromagnetic stress. Light striking a surface transfers momentum, so the field behaves as something that can push, even though the bookkeeping is done by fields rather than mechanical contact forces.

title: Observer-dependent split
body: Different inertial observers split the same tensor into energy density, flux, momentum density, and stress differently. The tensor is the covariant object; the component interpretation is frame-dependent.

title: Not a new electromagnetic field
body: The stress-energy tensor does not add a new field alongside \(F_{\mu\nu}\). It is built from \(F_{\mu\nu}\) to describe the energy and momentum carried by the electromagnetic field.

title: Electromagnetic momentum made local
body: The stress-energy viewpoint grew from efforts to understand electromagnetic energy flow, radiation pressure, and field momentum in a way compatible with relativity.

title: Takeaway
body: The electromagnetic stress-energy tensor is built quadratically from \(F_{\mu\nu}\). It gives the local density, flux, momentum, and stress content of the electromagnetic field.

title: Local energy-momentum bookkeeping
body: The energy-momentum tensor is the object that records how energy and momentum are stored and transported by fields and continuous matter.

title: Definition
body: The energy-momentum tensor \(T^{\mu\nu}\) is a rank-two tensor whose components describe densities and fluxes of energy and momentum. For an isolated system it obeys the local conservation equation \[ \partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{energy-momentum conservation}}{=}0. \] The \(\text{energy-momentum conservation}\) label marks the local balance law for energy and momentum.

title: What the indices mean
body: Roughly, one index says the direction in spacetime through which something flows, and the other says which component of energy-momentum is being transported. \(T^{00}\) is energy density; mixed time-space components encode energy flux or momentum density; spatial-spatial components encode stresses.

title: Origin in translation symmetry
body: The tensor is derived from spacetime translation symmetry using \cref{Noether's theorem}{sr.noether_theorem}. Time translation symmetry gives energy conservation; spatial translation symmetry gives momentum conservation. Field theory packages the four corresponding conserved currents into \(T^{\mu\nu}\).

title: Canonical form
Conservation as flow
body: The equation \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}\overset{\text{energy-momentum conservation}}{=}0\) is a local balance law. The label marks conservation as flow: energy or momentum does not disappear at a point; any decrease in a small region is accounted for by flux through its boundary.

title: Canonical is not always final
body: The canonical tensor is not always symmetric, gauge-invariant, or the most useful physical representative. One can often add an improvement term with identically vanishing divergence, preserving the conserved totals while improving the tensor's properties.

title: Electromagnetic example
body:
For the electromagnetic field, the useful symmetric tensor is built from the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}. In natural units and one common sign convention, \[ T^{\mu
u}\overset{	ext{EM tensor}}{=}-F^{\mu\lambda}F^
u{}_{\lambda}+ rac14\eta^{\mu
u}F^{\alpha eta}F_{\alpha eta}. \] The \(	ext{EM tensor}\) label marks the electromagnetic stress-energy construction in that convention. Its components contain field energy density, momentum density, flux, and stress.

title: Not just energy density
body: Seeing \(T^{00}\) as energy density is only the start. The tensor matters because it also records how energy and momentum move, and how momentum is transferred across surfaces as stress.

title: From conservation laws to tensors
body: The tensor form grew from nineteenth-century conservation laws and twentieth-century field theory. In relativity, energy and momentum cannot be separated cleanly, so their densities and fluxes naturally become one spacetime object.

title: Takeaway
body: The energy-momentum tensor \(T^{\mu\nu}\) packages local energy density, momentum density, fluxes, and stresses. Its conservation law expresses local energy-momentum bookkeeping.

title: Light as a field disturbance
body: Electromagnetic waves are self-propagating disturbances of the electromagnetic field, with electric and magnetic components locked together.

title: Definition
body: Electromagnetic waves are propagating source-free disturbances of the \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. In a chosen frame they appear as coupled oscillations of the \cref{Electric field}{sr.electric_field} and \cref{Magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field}, travelling at speed \(c\) in vacuum.

title: Source-free Maxwell equations
body: In a region where the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current} vanishes, source-free \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations} imply a \cref{Wave equation}{sr.wave_equation} for the field or for the potential in a suitable gauge. For the potential this can be written schematically as \(\Box A^\mu\overset{\text{source-free}}{=}0\). The \(\text{source-free}\) label marks that the current source has been set to zero.

title: Transverse fields
body: For a plane wave moving in direction \(\mathbf k\), the source-free divergence equations imply \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E\overset{\text{transverse}}{=}0\) and \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B\overset{\text{transverse}}{=}0\). The \(\text{transverse}\) label marks that both field components are perpendicular to the propagation direction.

title: The wave triad
body: In a simple plane wave, \(\mathbf E\), \(\mathbf B\), and the propagation direction form a mutually perpendicular triad. The direction of energy flow is given by the right-hand-rule direction of \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\).

title: Speed \(c\)
body: The source-free wave equation gives the dispersion relation \(\omega\overset{\text{wave equation}}{=}ck\). The \(\text{wave equation}\) label marks that the dispersion relation follows from the source-free wave equation. The speed is not a property of an ether-like medium; it is fixed by the electromagnetic equations and the spacetime structure of special relativity.

title: Energy and momentum
body: An electromagnetic wave carries energy and momentum. That is why light can heat a surface, exert radiation pressure, and transport energy across empty space.

title: Not two separate waves
body: An electromagnetic wave is not an electric wave plus an independent magnetic wave. It is one electromagnetic field disturbance whose components are related by Maxwell's equations.

title: Maxwell and light
body: Maxwell's theory predicted electromagnetic waves with a speed matching the measured speed of light. This was one of the decisive clues that light is electromagnetic.

title: Takeaway
body: Electromagnetic waves are source-free propagating field disturbances. In plane waves, \(\mathbf E\), \(\mathbf B\), and the propagation direction are mutually perpendicular, and the wave carries energy and momentum.

title: Finite-speed propagation
body: The wave equation is the mathematical pattern for disturbances that propagate through spacetime at a finite speed.

title: Definition
body: The relativistic wave equation uses the d'Alembertian \[ \Box\coloneqq\partial_\mu\partial^\mu\overset{\text{components}}{=}\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2 \] for the \(+---\) metric convention. The \(\text{components}\) label marks the coordinate expansion of the covariant operator. A source-free scalar component satisfies \(\Box\psi\overset{\text{wave equation}}{=}0\).

title: Metric structure
body: The operator \(\Box\) is built using the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}. Its time part and spatial part enter with opposite signs, encoding the light-cone structure of relativistic propagation.

title: From Maxwell equations
body: The electromagnetic wave equation is obtained from \cref{Maxwell's equations}{sr.maxwells_equations}. Writing the field in terms of the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} and imposing the \cref{Lorenz gauge}{sr.lorenz_gauge} gives, schematically, \[ \Box A^\mu\overset{\text{Maxwell + Lorenz gauge}}{=}\mu_0j^\mu. \] The \(\text{Maxwell + Lorenz gauge}\) label marks that this form uses Maxwell's equations together with the gauge condition.

title: Source-free region
body: When the \cref{Four-current}{sr.four_current} vanishes in a region, the potential equation reduces to \[ \Box A^\mu\overset{\text{source-free}}{=}0. \] The \(\text{source-free}\) label marks the condition \(j^\mu=0\). This is the clean wave equation for each component, subject to gauge and constraint conditions.

title: Plane-wave test
body: Trying a solution \(\psi\coloneqq e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) in \(\Box\psi\overset{\text{wave equation}}{=}0\) gives \[ -\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}+k^2\overset{\text{wave equation}}{=}0, \] so \(\omega\overset{\text{dispersion}}{=}ck\). The \(\text{wave equation}\) label marks imposition of the source-free equation, and the \(\text{dispersion}\) label marks the resulting relation between frequency and wave number. The disturbance propagates at speed \(c\).

title: Sources change the equation
body: The source-free equation describes free propagation. With sources present, the right-hand side is nonzero and the equation describes how charges and currents generate or drive fields.

title: Not every oscillation is a wave equation
body: An oscillating quantity is not automatically governed by a relativistic wave equation. The key structure is the coupling of time and spatial derivatives that produces propagating solutions.

title: Maxwell's prediction of light
body: Maxwell's equations led to wave equations whose speed matched the measured speed of light, supporting the identification of light as an electromagnetic wave.

title: Takeaway
body: The relativistic wave equation uses the d'Alembertian \(\Box\). In electromagnetism, Maxwell's equations in Lorenz gauge yield wave equations for the potential, with source-free solutions propagating at \(c\).

title: When the charge feels its own radiation
body: Radiation reaction is the correction to a charged particle's motion caused by the energy and momentum it radiates away.

title: Definition
body: Radiation reaction is the back-reaction on an accelerating charged particle due to its own emitted \cref{Electromagnetic waves}{sr.electromagnetic_waves}. It modifies the motion beyond the applied \cref{Lorentz force law}{sr.lorentz_force_law}.

title: Energy-momentum balance
body: An accelerating charge emits radiation. That radiation carries energy and momentum, described locally by the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor}. Conservation of total energy-momentum then requires the particle's motion to reflect what has been carried away by the field.

title: External force versus self-effect
body: The ordinary Lorentz force describes how an external electromagnetic field acts on a charge. Radiation reaction asks a harder question: how does the charge respond to the field generated by its own accelerated motion?

title: Radiative damping
body: A driven charged oscillator radiates while it moves. Some work done by the driving force leaves as radiation rather than remaining as mechanical energy. The motion therefore behaves as if there is a radiation-related damping effect.

title: Not ordinary friction
body: Radiation reaction is not friction against a material medium. It comes from the particle's coupling to its own electromagnetic field and from energy-momentum carried away by radiation.

title: Runaways and pre-acceleration
body: Naive point-particle self-force equations can produce unphysical runaway solutions or apparent pre-acceleration. These pathologies signal that the idealization of a point charge and its self-field must be handled with care.

title: Effective-theory viewpoint
body: In practical regimes, radiation reaction is often treated as a small correction valid within an approximation. The goal is to preserve energy-momentum balance without trusting the point-particle idealization beyond its domain.

title: A long-standing classical problem
body: The self-force problem has a long history, including work by Abraham, Lorentz, Dirac, and later Landau and Lifshitz. It remains a useful example of how subtle classical field theory can be.

title: Takeaway
body: Radiation reaction accounts for the back-effect of radiation emitted by an accelerating charge. It is required by energy-momentum balance but is technically subtle for ideal point charges.

title: Same laws in every inertial frame
body: Lorentz invariance is the precise mathematical form of the claim that no inertial frame is privileged in the laws of physics.

title: Definition
body: Lorentz invariance means that physical laws have the same form in all inertial frames related by \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}. Equations are written using objects that transform consistently, with invariant scalars unchanged.

title: Relativity principle made mathematical
body: The \cref{Principle of relativity}{sr.principle_of_relativity} says inertial frames are physically equivalent. Lorentz invariance is the mathematical implementation of that principle in spacetime: the allowed frame changes are those preserving the Minkowski interval.

title: Metric preservation
body: A Lorentz transformation \(\Lambda\) preserves the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}: \[ \Lambda^T\eta\Lambda\overset{\text{Lorentz}}{=}\eta. \] The \(\text{Lorentz}\) label marks the metric-preservation condition that defines Lorentz transformations. Therefore scalar products such as \(A^\mu B_\mu\) have the same value in every Lorentz-related inertial frame.

title: Writing covariant equations
body: Tensor notation makes Lorentz invariance visible. If both sides of an equation are tensors of the same type, changing frame transforms both sides in the same way. The component values may change, but the equation remains true.

title: Examples across the atlas
body: \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors}, the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor}, and the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} are standard Lorentz-covariant objects. They let mechanics and electromagnetism be written without choosing a preferred inertial frame.

title: Invariant is not the same as unchanged components
body: A scalar invariant has the same value for all inertial observers. A vector or tensor usually has different components in different frames. Lorentz invariance requires consistent transformation of the law, not identical component lists.

title: Why electromagnetism fits
body: Electric and magnetic fields mix under Lorentz transformations, but the electromagnetic field tensor transforms as one object. This is why Maxwell theory can be Lorentz-invariant even though \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) separately look frame-dependent.

title: Not an optional decoration
body: Lorentz invariance is not merely a pretty way to rewrite equations. In special relativity it is a basic constraint on candidate laws: a law that singles out one inertial frame needs a physical reason or it is suspect.

title: From covariance to spacetime structure
body: Lorentz covariance first emerged from attempts to understand electromagnetism and the transformations between moving observers. Einstein's formulation and Minkowski's spacetime geometry made the invariance principle structural.

title: Takeaway
body: Lorentz invariance says the laws keep their form under Lorentz transformations. It is expressed by metric preservation, invariant contractions, and tensor equations that transform consistently between inertial frames.

title: Choosing one description from many
body: Gauge fixing is the practical step of choosing one representative from a family of gauge-equivalent potentials.

title: Definition
body: Gauge fixing is the imposition of an extra condition on the \cref{Vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} to remove redundant descriptive freedom associated with \cref{Gauge invariance}{sr.gauge_invariance}. It should not change the physical field.

title: Why it is needed
body: Gauge invariance means many potentials can represent the same \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and the same \cref{Electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field}. Without choosing a representative, calculations can carry redundant variables that obscure the physical content.

title: Representative, not new physics
body: A gauge condition is like choosing a convenient representative from an equivalence class. It is not supposed to select a physically different electromagnetic field; it selects a cleaner description of the same field.

title: Lorenz gauge example
body: The \cref{Lorenz gauge}{sr.lorenz_gauge} imposes \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\overset{\text{Lorenz gauge}}{=}0\). The \(\text{Lorenz gauge}\) label marks this as a gauge choice. It is useful because it respects \cref{Lorentz invariance}{sr.lorentz_invariance} and simplifies Maxwell's equations for the potential into wave-equation form.

title: Residual freedom can remain
body: Gauge fixing does not always remove every redundant degree of freedom. In Lorenz gauge, a further transformation \(A_\mu\rightarrow A_\mu+\partial_\mu\Lambda\) preserves the condition when \(\Box\Lambda\overset{\text{residual gauge}}{=}0\). The \(\text{residual gauge}\) label marks the extra condition on the gauge function.

title: Keep observables gauge-invariant
body: After fixing a gauge, physical predictions should still be expressible in gauge-invariant terms. If a result changes under a remaining gauge transformation, it may be a description-dependent quantity rather than an observable.

title: Coordinate analogy and its limit
body: Gauge fixing is similar in spirit to choosing coordinates: a convenient description can make a calculation simpler. The analogy is not perfect, because gauge redundancy acts on field variables rather than directly on spacetime labels.

title: Not an extra law of nature
body: A gauge condition is not a new dynamical law. It does not add a force, remove the field, or change the charge distribution. It removes redundancy from the description.

title: From electromagnetic convenience to gauge theory
body: In classical electromagnetism gauge fixing was a calculational convenience for potentials. In modern field theory, gauge choice remains essential but must be handled so that physical predictions remain gauge-independent.

title: Takeaway
body: Gauge fixing chooses a convenient potential representative within a gauge-equivalent family. It simplifies calculation while leaving the physical electromagnetic field and gauge-invariant predictions unchanged.

title: Local Euclidean spaces
body: A manifold is the mathematical setting for a space that may be curved or globally complicated while still looking locally like ordinary coordinate space. In GR the spacetime arena is modelled as a four-dimensional smooth manifold before a metric is added.

title: Definition
body: A smooth manifold is a set that can be covered by coordinate patches whose overlaps are related by smooth \cref{Coordinate transformations}{math.coordinate_transformation}. The definition separates the idea of nearby points and smooth functions from any particular measuring rule for distance or time.

title: Coordinates as labels
body: A coordinate chart assigns numbers to points in some local region of a manifold. The numbers are labels rather than physical structure: changing the chart changes the component description without changing the underlying point.

title: Definition
body: A coordinate chart on a manifold is a one-to-one map from an open region of the manifold to an open region of \(\mathbb R^n\). An atlas is a collection of compatible charts whose overlaps are related by \cref{Coordinate transformations}{math.coordinate_transformation}.

title: Changing labels, not points
body: A coordinate transformation changes the numerical labels assigned to manifold points while leaving the points themselves unchanged. In GR this freedom is larger than the Lorentz transformations of SR: curved spacetime generally needs arbitrary smooth changes between local coordinate charts.

title: Definition
body: Given two overlapping charts \(x^\mu\) and \(x'^\mu\), a coordinate transformation is the smooth transition rule \(x'^\mu\coloneqq x'^\mu(x)\) on the overlap. The inverse rule \(x^\mu=x^\mu(x')\) lets the same point be described in either coordinate system.

title: Jacobian of the change
body: The derivatives \(\partial x'^\mu/\partial x^\nu\) form the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation. Later tensor components will use this Jacobian to change their numerical components while preserving the underlying geometric object.

title: Lorentz transformations as a special case
body: The \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} are special coordinate transformations between inertial frames in flat spacetime. General coordinate transformations need not be linear, global, or tied to inertial observers.

title: Not a change of physics
body: Changing coordinates is not the same as changing the physical situation. A badly chosen coordinate system can make simple geometry look complicated, and a well chosen one can simplify a calculation, but neither changes the manifold point or the coordinate-independent statement being described.

title: A history through spacetime
body: A worldline is the curve traced by a particle, observer, clock, detector, or light signal through spacetime. It turns a sequence of \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event} into one geometric object.

title: Definition
body: A worldline is a parametrized curve \(x^\mu(\lambda)\) in spacetime. The parameter \(\lambda\) labels points along the curve; for a massive clock or particle it is often convenient to use \cref{Proper time}{sr.proper_time} \(\tau\).

title: Curve versus coordinate plot
body: The worldline is the underlying curve, not just its appearance on a particular diagram. A \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} or a curved-spacetime coordinate chart can display the same worldline with different coordinate shapes.

title: Tangent direction
body: At each sufficiently smooth point of a worldline there is a tangent vector. In SR this tangent becomes the \cref{Velocity four-vector}{sr.velocity_four_vector} when the curve is parametrized by proper time; in GR the same idea lives in the local tangent space at the event.

title: Timelike and null cases
body: Massive particles and physical clocks follow timelike worldlines. Light follows null worldlines. Spacelike curves can appear in diagrams, but they do not represent the history of a material object or signal.

title: Vector space at a point
body: The tangent space is the local vector space attached to a point of a manifold. It is where velocities, infinitesimal displacements, and \cref{Worldline}{math.worldline} tangents live once there is no longer a single global vector space for all of spacetime.

title: Definition
body: The tangent space \(T_pM\) at a point \(p\) is the vector space of tangent vectors at that point. In coordinates its basis vectors are often written \(\partial/\partial x^\mu\), but the tangent vector itself is a geometric object independent of the chosen coordinates.

title: Dual vectors at a point
body: The cotangent space is the dual partner of the \cref{Tangent space}{math.tangent_space}. Its elements, called covectors or one-forms, act on tangent vectors and return numbers.

title: Definition
body: The cotangent space \(T_p^*M\) at a point \(p\) is the vector space of linear maps from tangent vectors in \(T_pM\) to real numbers. If \(v\in T_pM\) and \(\omega\in T_p^*M\), their natural pairing is written \(\omega(v)\).

title: Gradient as a covector
body: The differential \(df\) of a scalar function \(f\) is a standard covector example. It takes a tangent vector \(v\) and returns the directional rate of change of \(f\) along \(v\).

title: Dual basis
body: If \(\partial/\partial x^\mu\) is the coordinate basis for tangent vectors, the dual covector basis is written \(dx^\mu\). The basis is defined by \(dx^\mu(\partial/\partial x^\nu)\coloneqq\delta^\mu{}_\nu\).

title: Do not assume the metric too soon
body: Tangent vectors and covectors are distinct before a metric is chosen. A metric can relate them by raising and lowering indices, but the cotangent space itself does not depend on already having a measuring rule.

title: Tensors varying over spacetime
body: A tensor field assigns a tensor to each point of a manifold. GR uses tensor fields because equations must be meaningful under arbitrary smooth coordinate changes rather than only Lorentz transformations between inertial frames.

title: Definition
body: A tensor field is a smoothly varying assignment of multilinear maps or tensor products of \cref{Tangent spaces}{math.tangent_space} and \cref{Cotangent spaces}{math.cotangent_space} to points of a manifold. Scalar fields and vector fields are low-rank examples.

title: Point-by-point objects
body: The word field means that the object is assigned point by point. In GR the metric, stress-energy, and curvature are not single global arrays; they are geometric objects that can vary from event to event.

title: Scalars, vectors, and higher tensors
body: A scalar field assigns one number to each point. A vector field assigns a tangent vector. Higher-rank tensor fields have several vector or covector slots and can represent objects such as the spacetime metric or stress-energy tensor.

title: Not just an array of components
body: A tensor field has components in a chosen chart, but it is not merely that component array. Under a \cref{Coordinate transformation}{math.coordinate_transformation}, the components change in a controlled way while the underlying geometric object remains the same.

title: Indices as bookkeeping
body: Index notation compresses tensor statements, but an index can play two roles. It can record the abstract type of tensor slot, or it can label a numerical component after a coordinate basis has been chosen.

title: Definition
body: Abstract index notation writes objects such as \(T^a{}_b\) to show tensor type and contractions without choosing coordinates. Component index notation writes objects such as \(T^\mu{}_\nu\) for the components of that tensor in a selected coordinate system or frame.

title: Component indices
body: This atlas usually uses Greek indices such as \(\mu,\nu,\alpha,\beta\) for spacetime components. Unless otherwise stated, these indices range over the spacetime coordinates of the chart being used.

title: Repeated and free indices
body: A repeated upper/lower index pair is summed over. A free index must appear consistently on both sides of an equation. A repeated index is a dummy label: it can be renamed without changing the meaning of the expression.

title: Indexed need not mean coordinate-bound
body: An equation can be coordinate-independent even when it is written using indices. The test is not whether indices appear, but whether the objects and contractions have the right tensor transformation behaviour.

title: Components that transform correctly
body: The tensor transformation law is the rule that tells how component arrays change when coordinates change. It is what lets a tensor equation keep the same geometric meaning in different charts.

title: Definition
body: A tensor transformation law gives one Jacobian factor for each index when moving between coordinates. Contravariant indices transform with derivatives of the new coordinates with respect to the old; covariant indices transform with derivatives of the old coordinates with respect to the new.

title: Vector and covector cases
body:
For a vector, \[ V'^\mu \coloneqq  rac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^
u}V^
u. \] For a covector, \[ \omega'_\mu \coloneqq  rac{\partial x^
u}{\partial x'^\mu}\omega_
u. \] These are the simplest examples of the rule.

title: One factor per index
body: A higher-rank tensor receives one transformation factor for each index. The index positions are not decoration: they record which Jacobian or inverse-Jacobian factors are needed.

title: Not unchanged components
body: Tensorial does not mean the components stay numerically unchanged. It means the components change by the proper rule so that contractions and equations describe the same geometric statement.

title: A laboratory without weight
body: An accelerometer in a falling capsule can read zero even while the capsule accelerates towards Earth in ground-based coordinates. The equivalence principle turns this observation into a guide to gravity: freely falling laboratories provide the local setting for the laws of special relativity. The word local matters; it excludes comparing widely separated bodies over long times.

title: Universality and local physics
body: The weak equivalence principle states that ideal test bodies released at the same event with the same velocity fall alike, independently of composition. In Newtonian language their acceleration is \(\mathbf a=(m_g/m_i)\mathbf g\); universality makes the ratio common, and a choice of mass units sets \(m_g\overset{\text{mass convention}}{=}m_i\). This equality compares gravitational response with inertial resistance, not two separately derived formulas.

title: The Einstein principle
body: The Einstein equivalence principle adds that local nongravitational experiments in a freely falling, nonrotating laboratory obey special relativity, independently of its location and velocity. A supported laboratory feels weight because its floor prevents free fall. An accelerating laboratory in flat spacetime can reproduce that local experience without requiring spacetime curvature.

title: What a falling experiment tests
body: Release two small bodies beside an accelerometer inside a freely falling capsule. Neglect air drag, charge forces, spin effects and their own gravity. Locally they float together. Repeat the experiment with a larger separation and sensitive instruments: converging or diverging trajectories reveal \cref{tidal gravity}{gr.tidal_gravity}. Equal free-fall response does not imply equal motion for bodies subject to different nongravitational forces.

title: What the principle does not prove
body: The equivalence principle motivates a metric description, but does not by itself derive Einstein's field equations. Nor can it remove curvature over a finite laboratory. Strong-equivalence statements involving self-gravitating bodies are stronger than the local nongravitational principle used here. See \cref{local inertial frames}{gr.local_inertial_frame} for its coordinate expression.

title: Coordinates adapted to free fall
body: An SR inertial frame covers flat spacetime. In a curved spacetime its replacement is a local inertial frame at a regular event. It makes the coordinate description match measurements by a freely falling observer there, while leaving neighbouring tidal effects intact.

title: The conditions at an event
body:
Choose coordinates centred on an event \(p\), with an orthonormal basis and the atlas signature \(+---\). Local inertial coordinates satisfy \[g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{local frame}}{=}\eta_{\mu
u},\qquad \partial_ho g_{\mu
u}(p)\overset{	ext{normal coordinates}}{=}0.\] The labels identify coordinate choices, not field equations. Consequently the Levi-Civita connection coefficients vanish at that event.

title: A point is not a region
body: The metric near the event differs from its Minkowski value at quadratic order in the coordinate displacement. Curvature determines the leading departure; it cannot generally be removed along with the first derivatives. Approximating a laboratory by one inertial frame requires its size and duration to be small compared with the scales on which tidal effects become significant.

title: Free fall and hovering
body: A coasting astronaut can carry a nonrotating local frame whose accelerometer reads zero. A hovering astronaut must fire a rocket and has nonzero proper acceleration, even if their spatial coordinates stay fixed. Being momentarily at rest in some coordinates is therefore not the criterion for an inertial laboratory.

title: Orthonormal is not automatically inertial
body: Making the metric Minkowskian at one point fixes the basis there; eliminating first derivatives also constrains how coordinates extend nearby. An accelerated observer has an instantaneous orthonormal frame but not an inertial laboratory over time. \cref{Local flatness}{gr.local_flatness} states the geometric result; the \cref{equivalence principle}{gr.equivalence_principle} connects it to physical experiments.

title: The observer's accelerometer
body: Free fall means that an ideal small body experiences no nongravitational force. It includes an orbiting spacecraft as well as a dropped object. The operational test is an accelerometer carried with the observer, not whether its position changes relative to the ground.

title: A timelike geodesic observer
body:
A freely falling observer follows a timelike worldline with tangent \(u^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d	au\). In the test-body approximation its covariant acceleration obeys \[a^\mu\coloneqq u^
u
abla_
u u^\mu\overset{	ext{free fall}}{=}0.\] Proper time \(	au\) is the observer's clock time. The first relation defines acceleration geometrically; the second imposes the force-free motion law.

title: Coordinate acceleration can remain
body: The connection contributes to covariant acceleration, so \(a^\mu=0\) does not generally imply \(d^2x^\mu/d\tau^2=0\). Ground-based coordinates describe a falling object as speeding up. That description and the object's zero accelerometer reading are compatible because they measure different notions of acceleration.

title: Weight on a surface
body: A person standing on a surface is held away from a free-fall trajectory by the ground's contact force. Their accelerometer reads a nonzero value. Conversely, an orbiting astronaut can feel weightless while the spacetime curvature produces measurable tidal acceleration between separated parts of the spacecraft.

title: Limits of the ideal observer
body: Treat the observer as small enough that spin, finite size, radiation reaction and self-gravity do not alter the test-particle motion. The geodesic model is an approximation for real extended bodies.
