title: A static Newtonian source
body: For slowly moving matter with negligible pressure and anisotropic stress, a convenient isotropic weak-field chart gives \[ds^2\simeq(1+2\Phi/c^2)c^2dt^2-(1-2\Phi/c^2)\delta_{ij}dx^i dx^j.\] Here \(\Phi\) is the Newtonian potential and \(\Lambda\) is neglected. Both time and spatial components change; ignoring the latter loses part of the light-deflection result.

title: Gauge and approximation are different choices
body: A small coordinate change changes the components of \(h\), so their smallness is assessed in an appropriate chart, not every possible chart. Linearisation discards nonlinear terms after that choice. The \cref{Newtonian limit}{gr.newtonian_limit} adds slow motion and approximate stationarity; the \cref{post-Newtonian scheme}{gr.post_newtonian_approximation} keeps selected nonlinear terms consistently.

title: Recover both motion and the source law
body: The Newtonian limit requires a weak, approximately stationary field, slow test bodies and nonrelativistic sources whose pressure is small compared with rest energy. Set \(\Lambda=0\) for the ordinary Poisson law. Recovering acceleration alone is only half the check.

title: The metric gives the force law
body: With \(x^0=ct\) and \(g_{00}\simeq1+2\Phi/c^2\), the static connection gives \(\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq\partial_i\Phi/c^2\). The dominant part of the spatial geodesic equation is therefore \[\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}\simeq-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}\simeq-\partial_i\Phi.\] Slow motion suppresses terms involving spatial velocities; weak fields let proper time and coordinate time agree to the required order.

title: The field equation gives Poisson's law
body:
For a static weak perturbation, \(R_{00}\simeq
abla^2\Phi/c^2\). For low-pressure matter, \(T_{00}\simeqho c^2\) and \(T\simeqho c^2\), where \(ho\) is mass density. The \cref{trace-reversed equation}{gr.trace_reversed_equations} then gives \[ rac{
abla^2\Phi}{c^2}\simeq rac{\kappa}{2}ho c^2,\qquad
abla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi Gho.\] This fixes \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\) by matching Newtonian gravity.

title: An isolated spherical source
body: Outside the source, spherical symmetry and zero potential at infinity give \(\Phi=-GM/r\) in Newtonian theory. Its gradient produces inward acceleration \(-GM\mathbf x/r^3\). Inserting this potential into \(g_{00}\) also predicts the leading slowing of stationary clocks nearer the mass.

title: Keep the limits distinct
body: Small potential does not make light slow or radiation pressure negligible. The Newtonian motion approximation fails for light, even when linearised gravity remains valid. If \(\Lambda\) is retained, the same convention gives \(\nabla^2\Phi\simeq4\pi G\rho-\Lambda c^2\); the ordinary inverse-square result assumes that extra term is negligible.

title: Compare emission and reception clocks
body: A light signal exchanged by stationary observers in a static gravitational field can have different measured frequencies at its endpoints. The comparison concerns their proper-time rates; each observer still measures local vacuum light speed \(c\).

title: Stationary proper-time rates
body: Write the static metric with \(x^0=ct\), zero time-space cross terms, and \(g_{00}>0\) along the stationary observers. At fixed spatial coordinates, \[d\tau\overset{\text{stationary observer}}{=}\sqrt{g_{00}}\,dt.\] The common coordinate time is tied to the static symmetry; it is not itself the reading of every clock.

title: Use successive wave crests
body: Time-translation symmetry makes successive crests take the same coordinate travel time, so their emission and reception coordinate intervals agree. Dividing by the local proper-time rates gives \[\frac{\nu_B}{\nu_A}\overset{\text{static exchange}}{=}\sqrt{\frac{g_{00}(A)}{g_{00}(B)}}.\] Here \(A\) emits and \(B\) receives. This static formula is exact, not restricted to a weak field.

title: A small height difference
Do not apply the static formula to arbitrary observers
body: Motion adds Doppler effects, and a time-dependent geometry need not preserve the coordinate interval argument. Even a static chart ceases to describe physical stationary observers where its time direction becomes null or spacelike, as at and inside a Schwarzschild horizon. The conserved photon quantity associated with time symmetry is distinct from the energy measured by each local observer.

title: Follow null geodesics
body: In geometric optics, freely propagating light follows null geodesics of the metric. A weak isolated mass changes their direction relative to distant incoming and outgoing reference lines. No photon rest mass or material refractive medium is required.

title: The weak scattering setup
body: Take a static spherical mass \(M\), source and observer far away, and impact parameter \(b\) with \(GM/(bc^2)\ll1\). The impact parameter is the offset of the incoming asymptotic line, equal to closest approach only at leading order. Ignore rotation, other masses and cosmological curvature.

title: The full weak metric doubles the gradient term
body: From the isotropic weak-field metric and \(ds^2=0\), \(c\,dt\simeq(1-2\Phi/c^2)d\ell\). Thus the coordinate optical path has an effective index \(n\simeq1-2\Phi/c^2\). This is a computational description of geometry, not a local change in light speed. The transverse ray change is \(\Delta\mathbf e_\perp\simeq-2c^{-2}\int\nabla_\perp\Phi\,dz\) along the unperturbed line.

title: Integrate a point-mass potential
body: For \(\Phi=-GM/\sqrt{b^2+z^2}\), the magnitude of the leading bending is \[\alpha\simeq\frac{2GMb}{c^2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(b^2+z^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{4GM}{bc^2}.\] The ray bends towards the mass. In this chart, the time and spatial metric perturbations each supply half; that split is coordinate-dependent while the asymptotic deflection is observable.

title: Stay outside the strong-deflection regime
body: The result is first order in \(GM/(bc^2)\). Close to the photon sphere, multiple turns and capture require the full null-geodesic equations. A \cref{Newtonian slow-body calculation}{gr.newtonian_limit} cannot be applied to light to obtain the missing spatial contribution.

title: Radial and angular periods separate
body: In Newtonian inverse-square gravity, a bound test orbit is a closed ellipse. Schwarzschild geodesics add a small mismatch between radial oscillation and angular revolution, so the closest-approach direction advances. For other central bodies the same effect is called periapsis advance.

title: The orbit equation exposes the correction
body: Use \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), a test body, spherical nonrotating geometry and \(\Lambda=0\). Let \(q\coloneqq1/r\) and \(\ell\coloneqq r^2d\phi/d\tau\) be specific angular momentum. The timelike Schwarzschild geodesic equation reduces to \[\frac{d^2q}{d\phi^2}+q\overset{\text{Schwarzschild geodesic}}{=}\frac{GM}{\ell^2}+3mq^2.\] The last term is absent from the Kepler problem. The inverse radius is called \(q\) here to avoid confusing it with four-velocity \(u^\mu\).

title: Find the frequency shift
body: Write the leading ellipse as \(q_0=(1+e\cos\phi)/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\), with \(p_{\mathrm{orb}}\coloneqq a(1-e^2)\). Substitution into \(3mq_0^2\) produces a resonant \(\cos\phi\) term. Absorbing it into \(q\simeq[1+e\cos((1-\delta)\phi)]/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\) gives \(\delta\simeq3m/p_{\mathrm{orb}}\). Two periapses are therefore separated by slightly more than \(2\pi\).

title: Advance per radial orbit
body: The leading extra angle is \[\Delta\varpi\simeq\frac{6\pi GM}{a(1-e^2)c^2}.\] Here \(a\) and \(e\) are the leading Keplerian semimajor axis and eccentricity. The approximation requires a weak field throughout the orbit, especially near periapsis; the advance is positive for the Schwarzschild correction.

title: Separate other causes of precession
body: Other planets, a nonspherical central body and spin can also rotate the periapsis. The displayed expression isolates the test-body Schwarzschild contribution and omits radiation reaction. An exactly circular orbit has no unique periapsis direction; the nearly circular limit describes the mismatch between radial and angular frequencies.

title: Order corrections to slow orbital motion
body: Post-Newtonian (PN) theory extends Newtonian gravity with a controlled expansion for slow motion and a weak orbital field. It retains the nonlinear terms required at each order, unlike a calculation restricted to first order in the metric perturbation.

title: Choose an order-counting parameter
body: For a gravitationally bound system define \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\coloneqq v^2/c^2\ll1\). Virial scaling makes \(GM/(rc^2)\) of the same order. Newtonian dynamics is called 0PN; relative corrections of order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\) are 1PN and 2PN. This is order counting, not an exact equality between velocity and potential for every orbit.

title: Keep a consistent collection of terms
body: Obtaining 1PN motion generally needs \(g_{00}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^2\), \(g_{0i}\) through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}^{3/2}\), and spatial corrections through order \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PN}}\) in suitable coordinates. The components enter the motion equation multiplied by different velocity factors. Keeping the same power in every component would therefore miss contributions.

title: Conservative and dissipative corrections
body: Periapsis advance appears at 1PN. For nonspinning compact binaries, leading radiation reaction enters orbital motion at 2.5PN, relative order \((v/c)^5\), and causes secular energy loss. PN orders in a waveform or flux are counted relative to their own leading terms, so they should not be confused with orders in the acceleration.

title: Know the domain of the expansion
body: Near a merger or a horizon, slow-motion orbital expansion loses control. Widely separated compact bodies can nevertheless be treated using effective body descriptions even when their internal gravity is strong. Coordinate-dependent intermediate formulas must be compared using observables at the same retained order; more terms alone do not guarantee accuracy outside the approximation's regime. The orbital expansion describes the near zone; radiation at large distances requires matching to a wave-zone solution.

title: An exact spherical vacuum solution
body: Schwarzschild geometry solves the vacuum Einstein equations with zero cosmological constant and spherical symmetry. Its exterior is static even if a spherical source pulsates: this is the content of Birkhoff's theorem. Rotation, electromagnetic stress outside a charged body, or nonspherical radiation require other geometries.

title: Coordinates and signature
body: With \(+---\), define \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), \(f(r)\coloneqq1-2m/r\), and \(d\Omega^2\coloneqq d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\). The line element is \[ds^2=f(r)c^2dt^2-f(r)^{-1}dr^2-r^2d\Omega^2.\] The time coordinate is normalised to proper time of stationary observers at infinity. The exterior chart requires \(r>2m\).

title: Areal radius is not radial ruler distance
body: A symmetry sphere has area \(4\pi r^2\), which defines the geometric meaning of \(r\). Along a radial line on an exterior constant-time slice, the proper distance element is \(d\ell=dr/\sqrt{f}\). Thus coordinate radius is not generally the distance a chain of local rulers measures from a centre.

title: Read the weak-field limit
body: At large radius, \(f=1+2\Phi/c^2\) with \(\Phi=-GM/r\), recovering the Newtonian time component. The spatial part tends to flat spherical coordinates as \(r\to\infty\). At finite radius, the exact metric retains the nonlinear geometry needed for horizons and relativistic orbit structure.

title: A solution and its chart have different limits
body: An ordinary star's interior is not vacuum, so its material surface ends the exterior solution's physical applicability. For a black hole, \(r=2m\) is a failure of these coordinates; a \cref{regular extension}{gr.coordinate_singularity} crosses it. The singularity at \(r=0\) is a different, invariant problem. The static exterior description does not make the black-hole interior static.

title: Mass sets a length scale
body: The Schwarzschild radius translates a physical mass into a characteristic relativistic length. It locates the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole, but exists as a useful mass scale even for bodies whose surfaces lie far outside it.

title: The zero of the exterior lapse factor
body: Define \[r_s\coloneqq\frac{2GM}{c^2}=2m.\] The factor \(f(r)=1-r_s/r\) vanishes at this radius. The factors \(G\) and \(c\) convert mass to length: \([GM/c^2]=\mathrm{length}\). Doubling mass doubles the radius.

title: Compare scale with material size
body: For \(M\simeq2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\), using \(G\simeq6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) and \(c\simeq3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(r_s\simeq3.0\,\mathrm{km}\). A star of this mass can have a much larger material radius, so its exterior region never reaches this formal zero.

title: Compactness measures the regime
body: For material surface areal radius \(R_*\), define compactness \(\mathcal C\coloneqq GM/(R_*c^2)\). Then \(r_s/R_*=2\mathcal C\). Small compactness supports a weak-field surface treatment; approaching the Schwarzschild horizon scale requires fully relativistic reasoning and an appropriate model of the interior or collapse.

title: Escape-speed arithmetic is only a mnemonic
body: Setting the Newtonian escape speed to \(c\) reproduces the same expression, but Newtonian mechanics cannot derive a relativistic causal boundary. The \cref{event horizon}{gr.event_horizon} is established by the metric's causal structure. For rotating or charged black holes the horizon formula changes; \(2GM/c^2\) remains a mass scale rather than their general horizon radius.

title: A boundary defined by escape
body: For an asymptotically flat black-hole spacetime, the future event horizon bounds the region from which no future-directed causal signal can reach future null infinity. It is a global property of the entire causal geometry, not a material surface.

title: The Schwarzschild future horizon
body: In the black-hole extension of Schwarzschild, the future horizon lies at areal radius \(r=2m\). It is a null hypersurface generated by light rays. Outside it some future light rays can escape; on it the outward generators remain on the horizon; inside the black-hole region all future causal paths head to smaller areal radius.

title: Use coordinates that cross the horizon
body: Set \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\). In ingoing coordinates \(v\), the radial metric is \(ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr\), with \(f=1-2m/r\). Radial null paths obey either \(dv=0\) (ingoing) or \[\frac{dr}{dv}\overset{\text{outgoing null}}{=}\frac{f}{2}.\] The latter derivative is positive outside, zero on the horizon and negative inside. Timelike futures lie between the two null directions, so crossing inward is possible but escaping back out is not.

title: Crossing need not be locally violent
body: The horizon's curvature is finite, and for larger Schwarzschild mass its curvature scale is smaller. A freely falling observer crosses in finite proper time. A stationary observer held just outside instead needs proper acceleration that grows without bound towards the horizon. These are different worldlines, not conflicting descriptions of the same acceleration.

title: A local observation cannot locate a general event horizon
body: The full future is needed to decide which events can send signals to infinity. Local trapped-surface or apparent-horizon criteria are useful but are not the definition used here. In a collapse spacetime, the event horizon need not wait for local curvature to become large. The classical causal argument does not address quantum evaporation.

title: A chart can fail on regular geometry
body: Divergent or degenerate-looking metric components do not by themselves establish a singular spacetime. Coordinates can cease to label events smoothly, as polar coordinates already do at the origin of a flat plane. Schwarzschild's horizon provides a physically consequential example.

title: Build a horizon-crossing chart
body: Use \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), \(f=1-2m/r\), and define \[r_*\coloneqq r+2m\ln\left|\frac{r}{2m}-1\right|,\qquad v\coloneqq t+r_*.\] Since \(dr_*/dr=1/f\), substituting \(dt=dv-dr/f\) into the Schwarzschild line element gives \[ds^2=f\,dv^2-2\,dv\,dr-r^2d\Omega^2.\] The divergent radial coefficient has cancelled exactly.

title: Check nondegeneracy as well as finiteness
body: The radial components are \(g_{vv}=f\), \(g_{vr}=g_{rv}=-1\), and \(g_{rr}=0\). Their two-dimensional determinant is \(f\cdot0-(-1)^2=-1\), including at \(r=2m\). Thus the metric remains nondegenerate and Lorentzian there. The full determinant is \(-r^4\sin^2\theta\); polar-axis zeros are the familiar angular chart issue.

title: An extension, not a regular old chart
body: The transformation is smooth on its overlap with the exterior chart but singular at that chart's boundary. The resulting ingoing metric extends smoothly across the future horizon, admitting finite tangent components for infalling paths. This demonstrates regularity more strongly than checking a few finite curvature scalars alone.

title: Coordinates cannot remove every singularity
body: At \(r=0\), the Schwarzschild Kretschmann scalar diverges, so no smooth chart change can make the classical curvature regular. Conversely, finite invariants alone are not a universal proof of extendibility. Distinguish chart failure, invariant curvature behaviour and geodesic completeness when diagnosing an apparent boundary.

title: The Schwarzschild interior reaches a geometric boundary
body: In the black-hole region of the classical Schwarzschild solution, decreasing areal radius is unavoidable along future causal motion. The boundary \(r=0\) is a spacelike singularity, not a material point waiting somewhere inside a static spatial cavity.

title: Invariant curvature diverges
body: With \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\), \[K\coloneqq R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\overset{\text{Schwarzschild}}{=}\frac{48m^2}{r^6}.\] It is finite at \(r=2m\) and diverges as \(r\to0\). Since a regular coordinate change cannot alter this scalar at an event, the central divergence cannot be removed like the horizon's chart failure.

title: A falling observer has finite remaining time
body: For a radial geodesic released from rest at infinity, the exact energy equation gives \(dr/d\tau=-c\sqrt{2m/r}\). Integrating the proper time from horizon to singularity yields \[\Delta\tau\overset{\text{this geodesic}}{=}\frac{1}{c}\int_0^{2m}\sqrt{\frac{r}{2m}}\,dr=\frac{4m}{3c}.\] This value depends on the chosen infall energy; it is not the universal lifetime of every interior observer.

title: Singularity means incomplete classical geometry
body: The singular boundary is not a regular event belonging to the spacetime manifold. In the general theory, singularity statements concern inextendible causal geodesics of finite affine length or proper time; they need not always involve divergent scalar invariants. Schwarzschild has both finite-time incompleteness and divergent curvature.

title: Do not turn breakdown into a microscopic model
body: Classical GR gives no regular matter state at this boundary or account of what replaces it. Quantum gravity may be needed, but a particular resolution is not supplied by the solution. The Schwarzschild spacelike singularity also should not be copied unchanged into rotating or charged black-hole geometries.

title: Use symmetry to reduce radial motion
body: Time-translation and rotational symmetry give constants along Schwarzschild geodesics. Choosing the orbital plane as \(\theta=\pi/2\) reduces the problem to radial motion in an effective potential. The potential is an algebraic aid, not a second gravitational field.

title: Fix the energy normalisation
body: Set \(c\overset{\text{units}}{=}1\), retain \(m\coloneqq GM/c^2\) as a length, and write \(f=1-2m/r\). For timelike motion define \(\mathcal E\coloneqq f\,dt/d\tau\) and \(L\coloneqq r^2d\phi/d\tau\). Here \(\mathcal E\) is energy per unit rest energy and \(L\) is angular momentum per unit rest mass in these units; both are constant along a geodesic.

title: Insert the constants into the norm
body: The proper-time normalisation gives \[1\overset{\text{timelike norm}}{=}f\dot t^2-f^{-1}\dot r^2-r^2\dot\phi^2.\] Multiplication by \(f\) and substitution yield \[\dot r^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)=\mathcal E^2,\qquad V_{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\left(1-\frac{2m}{r}\right)\left(1+\frac{L^2}{r^2}\right).\] Dots mean proper-time derivatives. Allowed radial motion has \(\mathcal E^2\geq V_{\mathrm{eff}}\), and equality gives a turning point.

title: Circular orbits and stability
body: A circular orbit needs both \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathcal E^2\) and \(V'_{\mathrm{eff}}=0\) at fixed \(L\). The latter gives \(L^2=mr^2/(r-3m)\). The outer minimum is stable for \(r>6m\); the inner maximum is unstable for \(3m<r<6m\). The limiting orbit at \(r=6m\) is marginally stable, the ISCO. A turning point alone is not a circular orbit.

title: Null geodesics have a different potential
body: For an affine parameter \(\lambda\), define the analogous constants \(\mathcal E=f\,dt/d\lambda\) and \(L=r^2d\phi/d\lambda\). Zero tangent norm gives \(V_{\mathrm{null}}=fL^2/r^2\) and \((dr/d\lambda)^2+V_{\mathrm{null}}=\mathcal E^2\). This potential has a maximum at \(r=3m\), the unstable photon sphere. Null constants change under affine rescaling, but \(b\coloneqq L/\mathcal E\), the asymptotic impact parameter, does not.
